items.prompt: Choose the word that makes a polite request.
items.sentence: ___ we borrow the tennis racquets for our lunchtime game?
items.hint: You are asking nicely for permission, not stating a rule.
items.explanation: May is the modal verb for polite permission. Must asks about obligation, while would and ought cannot form this polite request.

items.prompt: Choose the word that shows the rule is compulsory.
items.sentence: Passengers ___ remain seated while the bus is moving.
items.hint: Bus safety rules leave no room for choice.
items.explanation: Must is high modality and makes the rule compulsory. Might, could and may would turn a firm safety rule into a weak maybe.

items.prompt: Choose the word that shows something is possible but not certain.
items.sentence: The wattle by our fence ___ bloom early if winter stays mild.
items.hint: The word if shows nothing about the blooming is certain.
items.explanation: Might is low modality, so it suits something that is only possible. Must, will and shall would all make the early blooming sound definite.

items.prompt: Which sentence gives advice rather than a firm command?
options: You must wear your hat outside during term one.
You will wait outside the office until called.
You should try the new climbing wall at lunchtime.
Visitors must not open the aviary gate.
items.hint: Compare the modal verbs and find the one that suggests rather than orders.
items.explanation: Should offers advice that the listener may ignore, so it is medium modality. Must, will and must not all express firm commands.

items.prompt: Choose the words that tell us HOW the dancers moved.
items.sentence: The dancers twirled ___ during the grand finale.
items.hint: You need the phrase that answers the question how.
items.explanation: With perfect timing tells us how the dancers twirled, so it is an adverbial phrase of manner. The other phrases tell us where or when.

items.prompt: Choose the words that tell us WHERE the lizard was sunbaking.
items.sentence: A shingleback lizard was sunbaking ___ this afternoon.
items.hint: You need the phrase that answers the question where.
items.explanation: On the warm brick path tells us where the lizard was sunbaking, so it is an adverbial phrase of place. The others tell us how or for how long.

items.prompt: Which sentence begins with an adverbial phrase of manner?
options: After recess, we returned to our classrooms.
Beside the boat ramp, tiny fish darted about.
With a gentle nudge, Zara launched the model boat.
On Saturday morning, we tidied the garage.
items.hint: An adverbial phrase of manner answers the question how.
items.explanation: With a gentle nudge tells us how Zara launched the model boat, so it is a phrase of manner. The other sentences open with phrases of time or place.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: Riding to school is ___ than waiting for the crowded bus.
items.hint: Better already does the comparing job on its own.
items.explanation: Better is the comparative form of good and needs no helpers. Adding more or most doubles up the comparison, and betterer is not a word.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: Our border collie ___ the ball before it bounced twice.
items.hint: Catch is an irregular verb, so it refuses the usual -ed ending.
items.explanation: The past tense of catch is caught. Catched is a common mistake, while catching and catches do not match the past time of the sentence.

items.prompt: Which sentence contains a mistake?
options: We baited our hooks with fresh prawns.
Them fishing rods belong to my cousin.
Dad and I fished from the rock wall.
We released the flathead back into the water.
items.hint: Check the small pointing words that sit in front of the nouns.
items.explanation: Them can never sit in front of a noun. The sentence should say those fishing rods, because those points to plural things.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: Both ___ trumpets were polished before the town parade.
items.hint: Both tells you the trumpets have more than one owner.
items.explanation: The trumpets belong to two brothers, so the plural brothers takes its apostrophe after the s. Brother's would mean just one owner.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: ___ been drizzling since the second quarter of the footy match.
items.hint: Try swapping the missing word for it has.
items.explanation: It's is the contraction of it has, which fits neatly before been. Its without an apostrophe only ever shows belonging.

items.prompt: Choose the words that best complete the sentence.
items.sentence: We ___ at the stop for twenty minutes before the tram finally appeared.
items.hint: The waiting started long before the tram turned up.
items.explanation: Had been waiting shows an action already in progress before another past event. The other options clash with the past tense verb appeared.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: The pair of goggles ___ at the bottom of my swim bag.
items.hint: The main noun in the subject is pair, not goggles.
items.explanation: The subject is the pair, which is singular, so it takes was. The phrase of goggles adds detail but does not control the verb.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: Bianca sharpened her pencil and ___ the next chapter of her story.
items.hint: Match the second verb to the past tense verb sharpened.
items.explanation: Began is the simple past of begin and matches sharpened. Begun always needs a helping verb such as has or had.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: The ___ hockey team trains at our local oval on Thursdays.
items.hint: Women is already plural before any apostrophe is added.
items.explanation: Women is a special plural that does not end in s, so ownership is shown by adding an apostrophe then s: women's.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: Neither the driver nor the passengers ___ keen on stopping before sunset.
items.hint: With nor, match the verb to the subject closest to it.
items.explanation: After neither and nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Passengers is plural and the sentence is in the past, so were is correct.

items.prompt: Which sentence is written correctly?
options: The manual says to charge the drone until its light turns green.
The manual say's to charge the drone until its light turns green.
The manual says to charge the drone until it's light turns green.
The manual say to charge the drone until its light turns green.
items.hint: Check the verb after manual and every its for a sneaky apostrophe.
items.explanation: Says is a plain verb and needs no apostrophe, and its shows the light belongs to the drone. It's would wrongly mean it is.

items.prompt: Which sentence contains a mistake?
options: Our principal announced the winners over the loudspeaker.
The whole school clapped and cheered for ages.
Each finalist were given a certificate and a badge.
Later, the band performed two new songs.
items.hint: Check that every subject agrees with its verb.
items.explanation: Each is singular, so the sentence should say each finalist was given. The plural verb were does not agree with each.

items.prompt: Which sentence punctuates the speech correctly?
options: "Pack your paintbrushes," called Miss Doyle. "The art room closes at three."
"Pack your paintbrushes" called Miss Doyle. "The art room closes at three."
"Pack your paintbrushes," called Miss Doyle "the art room closes at three."
"Pack your paintbrushes," Called Miss Doyle. "The art room closes at three."
items.hint: Check the comma inside the quotation marks and every capital letter.
items.explanation: A comma sits inside the closing quotation marks, and called stays lowercase because it continues the sentence. The second spoken sentence then starts with a capital.

items.prompt: Choose the words that complete the sentence in the passive voice.
items.sentence: The time capsule ___ by last year's graduating class.
items.hint: The capsule had the action done to it by someone else.
items.explanation: In the passive voice, the subject receives the action, so we need was buried. The doer then appears after the word by.

items.prompt: Choose the word that completes the sentence in the active voice.
items.sentence: The wildlife carer ___ the injured wallaby to the animal hospital.
items.hint: In the active voice, the subject performs the action itself.
items.explanation: Drove is active because the wildlife carer does the driving. The options with was and is would wrongly make the carer receive the action.

items.prompt: Which sentence is written in the passive voice?
options: The whipbird called from deep in the gully.
Our teacher marked the assignments overnight.
The banner was painted by the art club last term.
The galahs squawked from the power lines at dawn.
items.hint: Find the sentence where the subject has the action done to it.
items.explanation: The banner did not do anything; the painting was done to it by the art club. A form of be plus a past participle signals the passive voice.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best joins the ideas.
items.sentence: ___ the campfire smoke stung our eyes, nobody wanted to leave the circle.
items.hint: The two ideas pull against each other, so choose a contrasting joiner.
items.explanation: Although introduces the subordinate clause and signals contrast: the smoke was annoying, yet everyone stayed. So and and cannot begin this sentence, and because reverses the logic.

items.prompt: Choose the punctuation mark that belongs in the gap.
items.sentence: Bring the following to Saturday's game ___ shin pads, boots and a mouthguard.
items.hint: A complete statement like bring the following needs a special mark before its list.
items.explanation: A colon introduces a list after a complete statement. A semicolon joins clauses instead, and a comma is too weak to introduce this list.

items.prompt: Choose the punctuation mark that best joins the two clauses.
items.sentence: Kelly trains at the velodrome on Tuesdays ___ her brother prefers Friday sessions.
items.hint: Two complete, closely related clauses need something stronger than a comma.
items.explanation: A semicolon can join two closely related main clauses on its own. A comma would create a comma splice, and a colon is for lists or explanations.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best suits a formal report.
items.sentence: Several students ___ that the music rooms open at lunchtime.
items.hint: A formal report avoids slang and chatty words.
items.explanation: Requested is precise and formal, so it suits a report. Reckoned, whinged and bugged belong in playground chat, not formal writing.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best suits a formal report.
items.sentence: Attendance records showed a ___ improvement across the term.
items.hint: Three of these words sound like excited playground talk.
items.explanation: Significant is the formal word for describing an important change. Whopping, mega and crazy are slang and would sound out of place in a report.

items.prompt: Which sentence correctly joins the two ideas using a subordinate clause?
options: The glue dried, we cut out the photo frames.
The glue dried we cut out the photo frames.
While the glue dried we cut, out the photo frames.
While the glue dried, we cut out the photo frames.
items.hint: When the subordinate clause comes first, a comma must mark where it ends.
items.explanation: While the glue dried is a subordinate clause, so a comma separates it from the main clause. The other versions are comma splices, run-ons or place the comma wrongly.

items.prompt: Which sentence is most suitable for a formal school report?
options: Heaps of parents rocked up to the working bee.
The working bee was totally epic this year.
Everyone was super pumped about the working bee.
Volunteer numbers at the working bee increased noticeably this year.
items.hint: Formal writing avoids slang like heaps, epic and pumped.
items.explanation: Increased noticeably uses measured, formal vocabulary that suits a report. The other sentences rely on slang that suits chatting with friends.

items.prompt: Choose the noun that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: Her clear ___ of the rules meant the new players never felt lost.
items.hint: After the describing word clear, the sentence needs a noun built from explain.
items.explanation: Explanation is the noun formed from the verb explain, which is called nominalisation. The verb forms cannot follow her clear.

items.prompt: Choose the noun that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: The gymnast's graceful ___ of the routine impressed every judge.
items.hint: The word graceful must describe a noun built from the verb perform.
items.explanation: Performance is the noun made from perform. Nominalisation turns actions into things and gives writing a formal tone.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The jaffle iron sizzled, lunch was ready.
The jaffle iron sizzled lunch was ready.
The jaffle iron sizzled; lunch was ready.
The jaffle iron sizzled; and lunch was ready.
items.hint: A comma alone cannot join two complete clauses, but another mark can.
items.explanation: A semicolon joins the two related main clauses correctly. A comma alone makes a comma splice, and a semicolon should never team up with and.

items.prompt: Choose the correctly punctuated title to complete the sentence.
items.sentence: The short story ___ won first prize in our writing competition.
items.hint: Short works like stories need quotation marks and capital letters together.
items.explanation: A short story title sits inside quotation marks with capitals on its main words. The other versions are missing the capitals, a quotation mark or both.

items.prompt: Choose the punctuation mark that belongs in the gap.
items.sentence: The tour guide announced___ "The observation deck opens at ten."
items.hint: A small mark must separate the speaker's words from the speech that follows.
items.explanation: A comma follows announced before the quotation marks open. Without it, the reporting words crash straight into the speech.

items.prompt: Choose the words that best complete the sentence.
items.sentence: By the end of camp, every student ___ the mountain-bike trail at least twice.
items.hint: You need a helping verb plus the special past form of ride.
items.explanation: Ridden is the past participle that follows had. Rode never follows a helping verb, and every student is singular, so have is also wrong.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: After an ___ drive, we finally reached the snowfields.
items.hint: The drive lasts one hour, and the little word an confirms it.
items.explanation: One hour of driving is written an hour's drive, with the apostrophe before the s. Hours' would mean the time belonged to several hours.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: Every one of the life jackets ___ checked carefully before the rafting trip begins.
items.hint: The true subject is every one, and the checking happens in the present.
items.explanation: Every one is singular, so it takes is. The plural life jackets sits inside the phrase of the life jackets and does not control the verb.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.sentence: After the long walk, our old greyhound ___ in the shade for hours.
items.hint: To rest flat somewhere is to lie, and this happened in the past.
items.explanation: Lay is the past tense of lie, meaning to rest. Laid needs an object, lain needs a helping verb, and lied means told a fib.

items.prompt: Which sentence is written correctly?
options: The rowing club's captain accepted the award and thanked her crew.
The rowing clubs' captain accepted the award, and thanked her crew.
The rowing clubs captain accepted the award and, thanked her crew.
The rowing club's captain excepted the award and thanked her crew.
items.hint: Check the apostrophe, the commas and the tricky word accepted.
items.explanation: Club's shows the captain belongs to one club, and no comma is needed between the two joined verbs. Excepted means left out, so it is the wrong word.
